items.title: An MRI scanner uses a 1.5 tesla magnetic field — 30,000 times Earth's
items.claim: A typical clinical MRI scanner has a magnetic field around 1.5 T; high-field research machines reach 7 T. Generating such a field continuously requires kilometres of niobium-titanium wire cooled by liquid helium to about 4 K, where it becomes superconducting and carries current with no losses.
items.prompt: Why are superconducting magnets used instead of ordinary electromagnets?

options.text: An ordinary copper-wire electromagnet generating 1.5 T over the bore needed for a patient would dissipate megawatts of heat — practical only for brief pulses; a superconducting magnet, once energised, carries the same current forever with essentially no power input
Superconductors produce stronger fields per amp
Liquid helium is required for the radio detection

items.reveal:
A superconducting magnet is energised once (the current is ramped up from zero) and the current loop is closed via a superconducting switch. The current then flows indefinitely with no resistive losses. The magnet maintains its field as long as the helium keeps the wire below its critical temperature.

Liquid helium boils away slowly. A clinical MRI typically uses a 'cold head' refrigerator to recondense escaping helium — losses are then near zero for years. A 'quench' (loss of superconductivity, often from a tiny warm spot) dumps the magnet's stored energy as heat in seconds, boiling the helium and venting it through emergency pipes.

MRI uses the magnetic field to align protons in the patient's tissue; radio-frequency pulses tip the alignment; relaxation back to the field emits signals that are spatially reconstructed into images.
items.why: Superconductivity is taught as a cryogenic curiosity. It is the technology that makes medical MRI imaging possible — and many particle accelerators.

items.title: A particle can pass through a wall it cannot climb
items.claim: A 1 MeV electron approaches a 2 MeV potential barrier. Classical intuition says it bounces back — it lacks the energy to climb. Quantum mechanics disagrees and the Sun depends on the disagreement.
items.prompt: What is the probability the electron passes through?

options.text: 0 percent — a hard wall is a hard wall
Around 50 percent — energy is roughly halfway
Tiny but non-zero — the wavefunction decays exponentially inside the barrier but doesn't reach zero, so there's a calculable probability of finding the electron on the far side
100 percent — quantum particles always pass through barriers

items.reveal_title: Quantum tunnelling and a wavefunction that never quite reaches zero
items.reveal:
The Schrödinger equation gives a non-zero solution for the wavefunction INSIDE a classically forbidden region. The amplitude decays exponentially with distance, but it doesn't vanish.

This is why the Sun burns. Proton-proton fusion at solar core temperatures (about 15 million K) is classically forbidden — the Coulomb barrier is far higher than the thermal energy of the protons. Without tunnelling, fusion would not happen, the Sun would not shine, and we wouldn't exist.

It's also how scanning tunnelling microscopes image atoms, how flash memory works, and how alpha decay happens.
items.why: Students picture barriers as walls. In quantum mechanics, a wavefunction is a probability amplitude — and it leaks through anything finite.

items.title: A hammer and a feather fall at the same rate — on the Moon
items.claim: In 1971, Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the lunar surface. With no air, they hit the ground simultaneously. On Earth, the feather drifts.
items.prompt: Why are objects in vacuum equally accelerated regardless of mass?

options.text: Mass cancels in gravity but not in air resistance — F equals mg gives a equals g for all masses, independent of m
Heavier objects fall faster, as Aristotle taught
The Moon's lower gravity equalises everything
Atoms of equal mass act equally regardless of vacuum

items.reveal_title: Equivalence of gravitational and inertial mass
items.reveal:
Newton's second law: F equals ma. Gravity: F equals m sub g times g, where m sub g is the gravitational mass. Setting them equal: a equals (m sub g over m sub i) times g. If gravitational mass equals inertial mass — and to date no experiment has distinguished them, to better than 1 part in 10 to the 13 (MICROSCOPE satellite, 2017) — then a equals g for all bodies.

Galileo allegedly demonstrated this from the Leaning Tower of Pisa (his student Viviani says so; the historical record is unclear). The Apollo 15 demonstration is recorded on video and unambiguous.

Einstein elevated the equivalence to a principle and built general relativity on top of it: gravity is geometry, and all objects in free fall follow the same geodesic regardless of mass.
items.why: Daily observation (feathers float, rocks drop) suggests heavier things fall faster. Air resistance is doing the work — gravity treats them all equally.
